question: What type of stimulus does the sense of smell detect?
explanation: Olfaction is a chemical sense that responds specifically to airborne chemical molecules entering the nasal cavity. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h1)

question: Why is the sense of smell so important for tasting food?

options.A: Taste buds on the tongue directly stimulate olfactory receptors
options.B: Saliva breaks down food chemicals into light waves for the nose
options.C: Odor molecules travel to the nasal cavity during chewing and swallowing
options.D: The stomach sends electrical signals to the olfactory bulb

explanation: As food is chewed, volatile molecules travel up through the nasopharynx to reach olfactory receptors, heavily shaping flavor. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h1)

question: Where is the smell-sensitive tissue located in the nasal cavity?
explanation: The olfactory epithelium sits high up on the roof of the nasal cavity, directly beneath the cribriform plate. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h2)

question: What is the special job of basal cells in the olfactory tissue?

options.A: They regulate body temperature inside the nasal passage
options.B: They send electrical signals directly to the temporal lobe
options.C: They secrete thick mucus to trap incoming dust particles
options.D: They divide to regenerate damaged olfactory receptor neurons

explanation: Basal cells act as stem cells that constantly replace worn-out or injured olfactory receptor neurons. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h2)

question: Which molecule acts as a second messenger to open ion channels when we smell something?
explanation: The activation of adenylate cyclase raises cyclic AMP levels, which opens sodium and calcium channels to depolarize the cell. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h3)

question: If a drug blocks adenylate cyclase in nose neurons, what happens?

options.A: Immediate destruction of all basal stem cells in the nose
options.B: Permanent physical damage to the cribriform plate
options.C: Inability to generate action potentials in response to smells
options.D: Excessive production of thick mucus in the nasal passages

explanation: Blocking adenylate cyclase halts the signaling cascade needed to open ion channels, preventing depolarization and smell perception. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h3)

question: Through which bone structure do smell nerve fibers pass to reach the brain?
explanation: The olfactory nerve fibers travel through the small holes of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h4)

question: What is the main job of glomeruli in the olfactory bulb?

options.A: They produce new stem cells to replace damaged olfactory neurons
options.B: They physically anchor the olfactory bulb to the frontal lobe
options.C: They secrete the protective mucus layer found in the nasal cavity
options.D: They serve as synaptic convergence points for specific receptor axons

explanation: Glomeruli organize incoming signals by collecting inputs from receptor cells expressing the same type of odorant receptor. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h4)

question: Which major brain relay station is skipped by smell nerve signals?
explanation: Unlike other special senses, olfaction projects directly to the cortex and limbic system without an initial relay in the thalamus. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h5)

question: Why do certain smells trigger emotional memories so quickly?

options.A: The thalamus filters out emotional data from all visual inputs
options.B: Olfactory receptor cells are actual extensions of the cerebral cortex
options.C: Olfactory pathways project directly to the limbic system and amygdala
options.D: Visual signals must travel slower because the eyes process light waves

explanation: Direct connections to limbic structures like the amygdala and hippocampus allow smells to trigger deep emotional and memory centers instantly. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h5)

question: What term describes getting used to a constant smell over time?
explanation: Olfactory adaptation is the fading of perceived odor intensity during prolonged continuous exposure. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h6)

question: Why is olfactory adaptation helpful for the human body?

options.A: It permanently destroys old receptor cells to make room for new ones
options.B: It stops volatile chemicals from reaching the delicate cribriform plate
options.C: It prevents sensory overload and keeps receptors alert to new smells
options.D: It directly stimulates the production of mucus in the nasal cavity

explanation: Adapting to constant background odors ensures the nervous system remains sensitive to sudden environmental changes or new hazards. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h6)

question: What medical term means a complete loss of the sense of smell?
explanation: Anosmia is the medical term for the total absence of the ability to detect odors. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h7)

question: A patient suffers a head injury that damages the cribriform plate. What symptom is expected?

options.A: Anosmia due to severed olfactory nerve fibers
options.B: Parosmia due to overactive basal cell regeneration
options.C: Hyposmia caused by chronic nasal polyp growth
options.D: Total loss of visual acuity from optic nerve damage

explanation: Fractures or shearing forces across the cribriform plate can easily sever the fine olfactory nerve filaments, leading to permanent anosmia. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h7)
